title: Emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots in InP nanowires: influence of quantum dot size, composition and nanowire geometry
authors: Tomasz Gzyl, Giada Bucci, Krzysztof Gawarecki, Elisa García-Tabarés, Anna Musiał, Valentina Zannier, Ylea Vlamidis, Fabio Beltram, Julian V. Montero, Beatriz Galiana, Lucia Sorba, Wojciech Rudno-Rudziński, Grzegorz Sęk
abstract: Hereby, we present an experimental and theoretical investigation of emission dynamics in zincblende InAsxP1-x quantum dots (QDs) embedded in InP nanowires (NWs) grown via vapour-liquid-solid mechanism by chemical beam epitaxy, using Au nanoparticles as a nucleation catalyst. By measuring time-resolved photoluminescence from an ensemble of QD-NWs it was possible to determine the exciton lifetime dependence on QD composition and height. Changes in the InP shell thickness surrounding the InP NW stem with a QD, brought additional insight into the influence of photonic environment on the carrier dynamics. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, combined with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, provided actual structural parameters. The experimentally obtained lifetimes were interpreted in the light of results of 8 band kp calculations combined with configuration-interaction model to take into account the Coulomb interactions and finite-difference time domain photonic simulations to include the effect of optical confinement. The full understanding of the experimental results required considering both, the changes in the QD potential and the Purcell effect, the latter leading to spontaneous emission inhibition in the case of NWs with thin InP shell.
summary: This research experimentally and theoretically examines exciton emission dynamics in semiconductor QDs embedded in NWs. By combining time-resolved photoluminescence with advanced simulations, the authors quantify how QD size, composition, and the surrounding waveguide structure modulate the radiative lifetime via the Purcell effect. This provides critical guidelines for engineering solid-state quantum light sources for telecom applications.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum dot (QD) emission dynamics, specifically exciton lifetime, are influenced by the QD size, composition, and the surrounding nanowire (NW) geometry.
main_result: The radiative lifetime is strongly dependent on the photonic environment; thin NW shells can cause significant spontaneous emission inhibition via the Purcell effect, while structural changes influence the intrinsic QD potential.
method: A combination of time-resolved photoluminescence measurements and advanced theoretical modeling, including 8-band k.p calculations, configuration-interaction models, and FDTD simulations for optical confinement, was employed.
model_or_system: The system involves zincblende InAsxP1-x QDs embedded within InP nanowires grown via CBE. The analysis considers the interplay between material properties (composition/size) and the photonic environment provided by the NW waveguide structure.
key_observables: Exciton lifetime ($	au$), Purcell factor ($F_P$), emission wavelength, and spectral dependence of these quantities.
important_parameters: QD composition ($x$), QD height, InP shell thickness (e.g., 55 nm vs 150 nm), and the resulting optical confinement modes ($	ext{HE}_{11}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires considering both changes in the intrinsic QD potential and the external photonic environment (Purcell effect) for a full understanding.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate PL spectra, measured decay times across different sample geometries (A, B, C), and calculated Purcell factors ($F_p$) as a function of emission wavelength.
paper_structure: The paper follows an experimental/theoretical cycle: structural characterization ($	ext{STEM}$/$	ext{EDS}$) informs the theoretical models ($\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$, CI) which are then used to interpret time-resolved PL measurements across varying NW geometries and QD parameters.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems by quantifying how engineered photonic environments (waveguides) modify fundamental quantum decay rates, a key concept in solid-state quantum emitters for quantum information.
